div.p: A worst case response time analysis exploiting precedence constraints between fixed priority scheduled tasks in tree-shaped transactions is presented. The algorithm extends existing methods for analysis of linear transactions allowing a wider range of systems, in which tasks may trigger more than one succeeding task on their completion, i.e. the transactions form trees. It also improves existing methods, producing tighter response time bounds for tasks in both linear and tree-shaped transactions. The improvement is due to better exploitation of the precedence relations between tasks, which also makes the analysis faster than earlier. Simulation results show a significant reduction of estimated worst case response times when compared to earlier analysis methods for both linear and tree-shaped transactions. Such improvement leads to less pessimistic schedulability tests for distributed fixed priority scheduled systems.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A large number of methods are available for response time analysis of task sets executing under a fixed priority scheduler on a single processor. Available analyses successfully handle e.g. systems with scheduler overhead [2], mutual exclusions between tasks [8] and precedence relations [1], to name a few. For systems with more than one processor, analysis in general becomes more complicated. For precedence related tasks in distributed systems, some analysis methods do exist [4][5] [10].

The derivation of tight bounds on task response times in distributed real-time systems is important, not only for testing system schedulability but also for providing realistic estimates to designers of e.g. control systems who may benefit from accurate knowledge of the timing behaviour of their control system implementation.

The analysis derived in this paper is based on the method WCDOPS (Worst Case Dynamic Offsets with Priority Schemes) presented by Palencia and Harbour in [5]. The method developed here, which we will call WCDOPS+, extends and improves WCDOPS in several ways. The extension is the support for branching transactions allowing tasks to have more than one immediate successor. This transaction type is common, for example in distributed control systems where multiple local controllers may be triggered by one centralized unit. The new analysis also significantly improves earlier algorithms. This is a result of a better exploitation of execution conflicts arising between precedence related fixed priority scheduled tasks. The conflict exploitation also makes the new analysis faster than its predecessors, since fewer execution scenarios need to be evaluated. This is particularly true when WCDOPS+ is compared to the only available alternative for analysis of tree-shaped transactions, WCDO [4].

Simulation results presented in section 4 show a significant reduction in response time bounds when WCDOPS+ is compared to WCDO. We also show that the response time bounds of tasks in linear transactions are smaller when WCDOPS+ is used instead of WCDOPS.

div.head: System model and basic notation
div.p: We study systems with multiple processors that execute tree-shaped transactions of precedence related tasks. The processors communicate via dedicated point to point connections or through communication buses that can themselves be modelled as priority scheduled processors. A transaction Γ i is activated by a sequence of external events that are periodic with the period Τ i . One particular instantiation of a transaction is called a job. We assume that different event sequences triggering different transactions are arbitrarily phased relative each other. Each transaction has a single root task that is released on the arrival of the external event, and that precedes all the other tasks in the transaction. We use τ ij to identify task number j of transaction Γ i . The root task of a transaction Γ i is always τ i1 , while the numbering of all other tasks in a transaction is arbitrary. A task τ ij is said to precede another task τ ik if τ ij has to complete its execution before τ ik can start. Such a precedence relation is denoted τ ij < τ ik . We have e.g. τ i1 < τ ik .

div.p: The immediate predecessor of a task τ ij is identified by pred(τ ij ) and is the task whose completion triggers the release of τ ij . Each task has one immediate predecessor except the root task who has none. The set of immediate successors of task τ ij is denoted succ(τ ij ) and contains all tasks that are released immediately on the completion of τ ij :
. We also define a sub transaction Γ ij of Γ i to be the sequence of all tasks preceding τ ij and τ ij itself.

Tasks are arbitrarily allocated to processors on which they are released in order of precedence and their execution scheduled by a pre-emptive fix priority scheduler. Multiple instances of a task that are active simultaneously are assumed to be scheduled in order of arrival. A task τ ij with worst case execution time and best case execution time , is allocated to a processor given by proc(τ ij ) with a priority prio(τ ij ). Tasks may use shared resources if these are protected by some synchronisation mechanism that bounds the maximum task blocking time, such as the priority ceiling protocol [8]. The maximum blocking time of τ ij due to such synchronisation is denoted B ij .

Similar to [5], we will during the analysis associate to each task τ ij a dynamic offset Φ ij and a dynamic release jitter J ij that are used to model tasks with precedence relations as if they were independent. Using this model, an instance of task τ ij that is executed in response to an event arriving at an instant t 0 , is said to arrive at an instant t 0 + Φ ij and is released after some delay that is upper bounded by J ij . Hence the latest time the instance of τ ij may be released is t 0 + Φ ij + J ij . Both the offset and release jitter may be arbitrarily large.

We seek to determine a tight upper bounds on the worst case response times for all tasks τ ij in the system. The response time, which is calculated from the arrival of the external event triggering transaction Γ i to the completion of τ ij , may be larger than the period T i . The bounds may be used for determining system schedulability if compared to the task deadlines.

div.head: Related work
div.p: The analysis method presented in this paper origins from the offset based analysis that was proposed by Tindell in [9] and later revised by Palencia and Harbour in [4]. It is also partly based on the holistic analysis by Tindell and Clark [10]. In Tindell's original paper, transactions are formed by independent tasks whose releases are separated in time by increasing offsets. No real precedence relations exist between tasks, and all offsets and jitters are fixed and known at design time. In [4], Palencia and Harbour presented the WCDO (Worst Case Dynamic Offsets) algorithm which extends the analysis suggested by Tindell. While Tindell's method handles tasks with static offsets and release jitters, Palencia and Harbour showed how it could be extended to find worst case response times for tasks with true precedence relations: Tasks with precedence relations are associated with dynamic offsets and jitters that are updated as results of earlier iterations of the analysis. Hence the analysis method is applied iteratively. The best case response time of a task becomes the dynamic offset of its immediate successor(s), while the difference between the worst and best case response times is their dynamic release jitters. Let , then a lower bound to the best case response time of τ ab is given by (2) and the dynamic offset and jitter are and

Other bounds of the best case response time are possible [7], but the one given in (2) will be used throughout this paper. Convergence is achieved, as noted in [10], through the relation that jitters increase with increasing worst case response times and the worst case response times increase with increasing jitter. Therefore, the iterations will converge to a stable solution if one exists. WCDO can equally well be applied to tree-shaped transactions. In a later paper, [5], Palencia and Harbour extend WCDO through more explicit consideration of the precedence relations between tasks in linear transactions. The resulting algorithm, called WCDOPS, is the base of the algorithm described in this paper.

div.head: Preliminaries
div.p: The analysis will be carried out by studying the contribution from different transactions to a task τ ab busy period containing one or more instances of the analysed task τ ab . A task τ ab busy period is an interval of time during which the processor is busy executing tasks with priority prio(τ ab ) or higher [3]. In an interval before the τ ab busy period the processor is either idle or executes a task with a priority lower than prio(τ ab ). A task that belongs to Γ i , that is allocated to the same processor as τ ab and that has a priority higher than or equal to prio(τ ab ) belongs to the set hp i (τ ab ):

div.head: Creation of the worst case scenario
div.p: In this section we will discuss how a transaction Γ i should be phased to contribute as much as possible to a task τ ab busy period starting at an instant t c . A task τ ik in Γ i is said to start the busy period for Γ i if it is released at t c after having experienced its maximum release jitter, J ik . It is shown in [4] and [9] that the maximum contribution from a transaction Γ i to a task τ ab busy period occurs when Γ i is phased such that some task τ ik in hp i starts the busy period. All tasks in hp i belonging to a job of Γ i should, if possible, be given release jitters such that their releases coincide with t c or occur as soon as possible after. This is the basic approach used to create the worst case for τ ab in all the methods discussed here. The remaining problem to derive which task τ ik that should be used to start the busy period will be handled later.

Figure 1 shows the execution of three jobs of a linear transaction Γ i with three tasks. Figure 1a shows how the tasks in Γ i would execute if there is no interference from other transactions in the system. Tasks are shown as boxes with their heights being proportional to their priorities. The dashed line shows the priority level of the analysed task τ ab . Downward pointing arrows show arrivals of the external events that trigger the start of the transaction and upward pointing arrows show the arrival of the individual tasks. Since the tasks execute undisturbed from other transactions, no jitter will delay the task release times.

Figure 1b shows the execution when the tasks are phased according to the worst case phasing described above when precedence relations are not considered and τ i3 is used to start the busy period. The relation between τ i3 's offset and maximum jitter and the beginning of the τ ab busy period t c , is indicated in Figure 1a. This scenario reflects the worst case assumption used in WCDO. Note how τ i3 from the first job and both tasks τ i1 and τ i3 from the second and third job contribute to the busy period in which τ ab executes. The length of the busy period is denoted w.

WCDOPS exploits the precedence constraints between the tasks in Γ i to reduce the pessimism in WCDO. One important contribution of WCDOPS is the identification and resolution of execution conflicts between tasks belonging to the same jobs. It is obvious that since the tasks in the example in Figure 1 are precedence related, tasks τ i1 and τ i3 from the same job of Γ i could not belong to the same τ ab busy period, since there has to be an execution of the low priority task τ i2 in between. This is reflected in Figure 1c which shows the worst case used in WCDOPS. Here, only task τ i3 from the second job is included in the busy period since τ i1 's execution time is shorter. Furthermore, due to precedence relations, only task τ i1 from the last job of Γ i contributes to the busy period.

In WCDOPS+ we note that since τ i3 in the first job belongs to the busy period, no other instance of τ i3 can execute within it. This is due to the fact that τ i2 , which is the immediate predecessor of τ i3 , belongs to lp i . When an instance of τ i2 completes it immediately releases τ i3 and a τ ab busy period starts. It is not possible for another instance of τ i2 to execute and release another instance of τ i3 until that τ ab busy period has finished. This constitutes a global conflict between transactions: There may be at most one task of all tasks in all transactions within a τ ab busy period that has an immediate predecessor in lp i . This conflict is exploited in WCDOPS+. In the example in Figure 1d the second job contributes with τ i1 instead of τ i3 resulting in a shorter busy period than in the other cases. The instance of τ i2 belonging to the first job has been placed next to the following τ i3 to highlight that it must complete at t c .

div.p: To properly identify and resolve execution conflicts for a transaction Γ i when the worst case response time for a task τ ab is analysed, the priority variation between tasks in Γ i needs to be considered. When task priorities within a transaction are not allowed to vary, the methods produce identical bounds. When priority variations are introduced in the transactions by increasing p prio , WCDOPS+ quickly becomes significantly better. div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have derived a method for response time analysis of tasks in tree-shaped transactions that exploits the precedence relations between tasks in a way similar to the earlier developed method WCDOPS for linear transactions. The new method produces much tighter bounds than the alternative method for tree-shaped transactions (WCDO), and tighter bounds than WCDOPS for linear transactions, when task priorities within transactions are not constant. The proposed method, WCDOPS+, therefore makes schedulability tests for both linear and tree-shaped transactions more accurate.

The function BranchInterference(τ ab ,τ ik ,τ iB ,w,p) (listed in Figure 4) implements the complete version of the recursive algorithm described above (15 to 17). The function produces two values: branchI, the maximum non blocking interference which is the interference achieved if no blocking H segment is allowed to contribute; and branchDelta, the maximum interference increase if the branch is allowed to interfere with a blocking H segment.

In BranchInterference, sectionI is computed as in (15) but with the difference that a function TaskInterference is called which returns either 0 or C ij depending on whether τ ij can contribute to the busy period or not. Furthermore, when a sub branch is analysed, using a recursive call to BranchInterference, two values are received in return: The sub branch interference (bI) is simply added to the interferences of the other sub branches (subBranchesI) as in (16), while the corresponding branchDelta is compared to those of the other sub branches and the largest one selected as subBDelta.

After the computation of sectionI, subBDelta and subBranchesI we check whether is a blocking H segment or not. If it is, sectionI only affects the branchDelta and the maximum non blocking interference of the branch becomes branchI = subBranchesI. The maximum interference increase is then calculated noting that the interference gained by letting the H section with the blocking H segment contribute to the busy period is sectionI -subBranchesI. This value must be compared to the interference increase achieved if we instead choose a blocking H segment in any of the sub branches: branchDelta = max(sectionI-subBranchesI, subBDelta).
If on the other hand, is not a blocking H segment, then the branch interference will be branchI = max(sectionI, subBranchesI) just like in (17), and the branchDelta is computed accordingly.

div.head: Simulation results
div.p: A large number of analyses have been performed of synthetically generated systems with both linear and treeshaped transactions. The analyses compare the estimated worst case response times of the WCDOPS+ algorithm with the response time bounds computed with WCDOPS for linear transactions, and WCDO for tree-shaped transactions. We used random systems with 10 transactions of 10 tasks in each, executing on 4 processors. The tasks were given rate-monotonic priorities (inversely proportional to the periods) with a random variation such that a task was given a completely random priority with a probability p prio . When tree-shaped transactions were analysed a task's immediate predecessor was selected in random. Normally a task was allocated to the same processor as its predecessor, but was moved to another processor with a probability of 0.2. The execution times of the tasks were scaled such that a pre-defined utilization was achieved in all processors. Five different systems were analysed for each utilization.
